column1: Less is more.|minimal,room,chair|Should we put another display by the entrance?~The existing one is clearer without it. Less is more.~Then we are removing clutter, not useful information?~Exactly. The essential directions must stay visible.|Would fewer signs always be better? Explain one case where this saying would not justify removing a sign.|No. Removing an essential direction could make the space harder to use.|Is one clear sign enough?~Yes. We do not need three.~Can people see it?~Yes. It is beside the door.|Does the door need three identical signs?|No. One clear, visible sign may be enough.

There is nothing in the world so irresistibly contagious as laughter and good-humour.|family,sharing,meal|Why does the narrator describe laughter as contagious?~Because one person's laughter can draw others into it.~Is the line a medical claim?~No. It is a literary comparison about a shared mood.|Explain contagious figuratively here, without presenting laughter as an illness.|Laughter can spread between people as a shared response; contagious is a metaphor.|Why are they all laughing?~One person told a funny story.~Did the others join in?~Yes. The good mood spread.|Does contagious mean an illness in this sentence?|No. It describes laughter spreading from person to person.

We need the tonic of wildness|seasons,uncanny,plant|What does tonic suggest in the passage?~Something that restores or refreshes us.~Is the writer prescribing a particular medicine?~No. The landscape is described as renewing the person's experience.|How does tonic shape the way wildness is presented?|It presents contact with wildness as refreshing or restorative rather than as literal medicine.|How do you feel after a walk outside?~A little more relaxed.~Is tonic a drink here?~No. It is a way to describe feeling refreshed.|Is the quotation describing literal medicine?|No. Tonic is used as an image for something refreshing.

Reading maketh a full man; conference a ready man; and writing an exact man.|library,book,notebook|Does conference mean a large formal event here?~It refers to discussion or conversation.~Then the three activities develop different capacities?~That is the contrast: reading, discussion and careful writing.|In this quotation, distinguish the older sense of conference from a modern conference venue.|Conference refers to discussion, not specifically to a large organized event or its building.|What are the three activities?~Reading, talking and writing.~Is maketh a modern verb form?~No. We normally say makes.|Give the modern form of maketh.|makes

brevity is the soul of wit|notebook,document,minimal|Should we cut every sentence in half?~Brevity is useful only if the meaning survives.~The line sounds simpler than the scene itself.~Yes. Polonius praises brevity while being notably long-winded.|Explain the irony of a long-winded character praising brevity.|The character's own speech conflicts with the concise speaking he praises.|Is the message long?~Very long.~Could it be shorter and still clear?~Yes. We can remove the repeated information.|Make this shorter: Please meet me at ten o'clock, which is the time of our meeting.|Please meet me at ten.

A thing of beauty is a joy for ever:|valentine,leaf,seasons|Why would a beautiful thing continue to give joy?~Its memory or influence may last after the first encounter.~Must everyone find the same thing beautiful?~No. The line invites reflection rather than establishing a universal preference.|Name one way an encounter with beauty can remain meaningful after the object is no longer present.|A remembered image, sound or experience can continue to evoke pleasure or significance.|Do you still remember that garden?~Yes. I liked the flowers.~Does the memory make you smile?~It does.|Name a beautiful thing you remember and one feeling it brings back.|I remember a garden in spring, and it makes me feel peaceful.

If music be the food of love, play on;|guitar,music,headphones|Why does the speaker compare music to food?~He imagines it feeding an emotional appetite.~Is that the same as saying music is literally edible?~No. The metaphor connects listening with desire and nourishment.|Explain the food metaphor without treating it as a literal definition of music.|The speaker imagines music nourishing or satisfying an emotional appetite.|Is music really food?~No. The speaker is making a comparison.~What can music give someone?~A feeling, rather than a meal.|Does food name something to eat in this quotation?|Not literally. It is an image for something that feeds a feeling.

Double, double toil and trouble;\nFire burn, and cauldron bubble.|cauldron,halloween-costume|Shall I whisper the whole chant?~Try stressing Double, double first. The repetition gives it a pulse.~And make burn and bubble sharper?~Yes. Let the repeated sounds help create the tension.|Identify one repetition and one repeated consonant sound, then suggest how an actor could use them.|Stress Double, double to establish a pulse and the b sound in burn and bubble to make the chant insistent.|What is a cauldron?~A large pot.~Are these words from a real instruction book?~No. They are spoken by witches in a play.|What object is named by cauldron?|A large pot.

I will honour Christmas in my heart, and try to keep it all the year.|christmas,sharing,family|Why does Scrooge say all the year?~He wants the change to outlast the holiday.~So the promise is about continuing conduct?~Yes. Its meaning depends on how he treats people afterward.|Suggest one action that could give practical meaning to keeping generosity beyond a holiday.|Continue offering considerate help during ordinary weeks, rather than limiting it to the celebration.|Does the promise end after Christmas?~No. He wants to keep it all year.~How could he show that?~By continuing to be kind to people.|Give one example of kindness after a holiday is over.|Help someone with a practical task during an ordinary week.
